papers.title: Splitting Planar Necklaces with Few Straight Cuts
papers.abstract: In the classical necklace splitting problem, beads of different colors lie on a line, and the goal is to divide them among $k$ agents using as few cuts as possible so that every agent receives the same number of beads of each color. We study the planar analog in which a cut is a full straight line and the objective is minimizing the number of lines: $m$ points colored red and blue must be separated by straight-line cuts into regions that can be allocated to $k$ agents so that each agent receives the same number of points of each color. Projection to a line gives $2(k-1)$ cuts, and $k-1$ are sometimes necessary; we give algorithms, static and dynamic, that provably close part of this gap. We develop several approaches that capitalize on the extra degree of freedom: a ``star'' search that produces solutions with as few as $\lceil \frac{k}{2} \rceil$ cuts and never more than $k$ whenever a fair contiguous circular partition exists, with further guarantees for evenly spaced input, and a general algorithm that produces at most $k + \log_2(k+1) - 2$ cuts in $\Theta(m \log k)$ time, built on a one-dimensional necklace splitting subroutine that requires no presorting. We then adapt the general algorithm to a dynamic setting, maintaining exact fairness and the cut bound under arbitrary relocation of points, with expected update time that scales with the total distance moved.

papers.title: A Short Note on Algorithms For The Noisy $k$-XOR Problem
papers.abstract: This mostly expository note studies the sample-noise regimes in which the testing problem for noisy $k$-XOR in dimension $n$ can be efficiently solved. Concretely, we ask what pairs $(\beta, \delta)$ admit algorithms running in time $n^{O(k)}$ where $m = n^\beta, \beta \in [0,k]$ is the number of samples and $\mathsf{Bern}(n^{-\delta}),\delta \in (0,+\infty)$ is the noise distribution. The current state-of-the-art algorithms are: I. A folklore algorithm when $\beta > 1, \delta>1$ based on Gaussian elimination; II. A folklore algorithm when $\beta\ge k/2$ based on the birthday paradox; III. A recent algorithm in the regime $\beta > \delta + k(1-\delta), \delta \in (0,1)$ based on a reduction to the first algorithm [DJ24,CSZ24]. IV. Extending [AF09], we strictly improve the last regime to $\beta > \delta + (k-1)(1-\delta), \delta \in (0,1).$ These algorithms correspond to efficiently finding short cycles in uniform hypergraphs and can be equivalently phrased as algorithmic Moore bounds.

papers.title: Deterministic Shift Equivalence Testing for Sparse Polynomials
papers.abstract: We study the shift equivalence testing problem for high-degree sparse multivariate polynomials. Given explicit spar se representations of two polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, with exponents encoded in binary, sparsities $s$ and $t$, and total degree at most $d$, the task is to decide whether there is a vector $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ such that $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{a})\equiv g(\mathbf{x})$. Furthermore, one needs to output such a vector if it exists. Dvir, Oliveira, and Shpilka (ICALP 2014) studied shift equivalence for low-degree arithmetic circuits. Their framew ork does not apply directly to sparse polynomials, which are not closed under shifts, and they left open whether shift equivalence of sparse polynomials admits an efficient deterministic algorithm. We answer this question positively over $\mathbb{Q}$. If the input coefficients have bit-size at most $\tau$, we sh ow that a rational shift of polynomial bit-size exists whenever the polynomials are shift equivalent. Moreover, our alg orithm outputs such a shift and has a running time of $\operatorname{poly}(n,s,t,\tau,\log d)$ in the bit model. The ar ithmetic and structural parts of our result also hold over any field of characteristic zero or characteristic larger th an $d$.

papers.title: A 55-Addition Rank-23 Scheme for $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication via Exact Two-Sided Minimization
papers.abstract: We give a scheme that multiplies two $3\times3$ matrices with 23 multiplications and 55 additions over any ring, one addition below the previous record of 56 (Sun, 2026) and the first below 56 for exact non-commutative $3\times3$ multiplication without a change of basis. The scheme forms 13 signed combinations of the entries of A and 14 of B, takes 23 products, and recombines them with 28 further additions; its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4. The previous records, from 60 down to 56, were obtained by greedy common-subexpression elimination, which only bounds each side of a scheme from above. We minimize both input sides exactly by chain covering, and the output side exactly through the transposition principle: the 9-by-23 output map costs its transpose plus 14, and the transpose is a 9-input map that the input-side minimizer solves exactly. Applied to Perminov's cn122 scheme (class i19w225c4efh, published at 58 additions) this gives 55 = 13 + 14 + 28, where greedy elimination reaches only 29 on the output side. The same method shows that Sun's representative is output-optimal at 56, and an exact orbit-wide computation over the Heule-Kauers-Seidl database shows that the record class is the only database class attaining 55.

papers.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
papers.abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.

papers.title: Subjective Valuations Make It Hard to be Fair: The Complexity of Resource Allocation to Groups of Agents
papers.abstract: We study the parameterized complexity of finding an EF1 allocation of indivisible items in the group-sharing setting, which has received increasing attention in recent years. There, items are not allocated to individual agents but rather to one of two (or possibly more) groups, and agents within that group all share the assigned items. We consider both the "fixed" (EF1-Fix) and "variable" (EF1-Var) group cases, where in the former the assignments of agents to groups are prescribed. While both are NP-hard in the classical sense, we show that their algorithmic behavior differs significantly from the parameterized perspective. As our main results, we: (1) prove that both cases are NP-hard even when the number of agents is a small constant; (2) circumvent this hardness by establishing fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Var w.r.t. the number of "subjective" items, that is, items which are viewed as chores or goods by different agents---but rule out an analogous result for EF1-Fix; and (3) establish fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Fix w.r.t. the number of item types, but link the existence of an analogous fixed-parameter algorithm for EF1-Var to a fundamental open question in the setting of Integer Linear Programming.

papers.title: CAFS: A Cache-Aware Frequency Sort for Low-Cardinality Integer Data on x86-64
papers.abstract: Integer sorts in OLAP engines often run on columns whose cardinality $K$ is much smaller than the array length $N$. After a group-by stage the intermediate key column has $K$ bounded by the number of distinct group keys, and even a column-store scan typically operates on dictionary-encoded categorical fields where $K$ never exceeds a few thousand. A comparison sort on such a column still pays $\Theta(N \log N)$ comparisons, and a radix sort still pays $\Theta(N \cdot B/b)$ byte passes, irrespective of $K$. This paper describes CAFS, an integer sort that does exploit it on x86-64 with AVX2. The algorithm combines a SIMD bucket sized to one cache line, a Chao1 cardinality estimator over 1024 strided samples (kept in a heap-allocated 40 KB open-addressing table), and an adaptive dispatcher backed by a spill safety guard. The hot loop is branchless and uses AVX2 cmpeq together with movemask and tzcnt to locate the matching lane. We benchmarked CAFS on a full-factorial grid of 58 array sizes $N$ from $10^3$ to $3 \cdot 10^7$ with dense $K$ schedules per $N$, producing 592770 timed runs against pdqsort, IPS4o, vqsort, ska_sort, and std::sort. In the $K \ll N$ band the throughput is 1.7 to 3.1x that of pdqsort, 1.7 to 3.5x IPS4o, and 1.2 to 2.3x vqsort. The operational crossover against pdqsort is at $K \approx 1.3 \cdot 10^5$; against ska_sort, $K \approx 8.14 \cdot 10^5$; against vqsort, $K \approx 6.7 \cdot 10^5$; and against IPS4o the curves only converge near $K = N$. Of the five baselines, only vqsort actually overtakes CAFS once the crossover is passed, which makes the vqsort threshold at $K \approx 6.7 \cdot 10^5$ the binding constraint on the operational range of CAFS.

papers.title: Optimal Algorithms and Hardness for Max-Cut in Bounded Degree Graphs
papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves an $\alpha_{GW} + \tilde{\Omega}(1/d)$-approximation for Max 2-LIN(2) in weighted instances where each vertex appears in at most $d$ constraints. This improves on the $\alpha_{GW}+\tilde{\Omega}(1/d^2)$-approximation guarantee of [Hsieh-Kothari, ICALP'23]. We also show a matching Unique Games hardness under randomized polynomial-time reductions, thereby proving that the gain on $\alpha_{GW}$ is optimal up to $\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ factors. Here, $\alpha_{GW} \approx 0.878$ is the approximation ratio of the Goemans-Williamson algorithm. Our results resolve an open question due to Raghavendra and refute his conjectured optimal approximation ratio of $\alpha_{GW} + \tilde{\Omega}(1/\sqrt{d})$. Our local improvement scheme can be thought of as using an adaptive (based on the neighbors) shift applied to the Gaussian before using the GW sign rounding. This allows us to implement a ``soft but simultaneous'' flipping decision at each vertex as opposed to hard but sequential flipping decisions in prior works. Our hardness results are based on a new sparsification lemma for graphs produced by the reduction from Unique Games [Khot-Kindler-Mossel-O'Donnell, SICOMP'07] that preserves the optimal values up to a factor of $1 \pm \epsilon$ while subsampling to an average degree of only $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon)$. This is the first example of a CSP in which the optimal advantage on degree-$d$ instances is asymptotically smaller than $O(1/\sqrt{d})$ [Trevisan, STOC'01]. A key idea in the proof of our sparsification theorem establishes new bounds on the number of ``nearly optimal'' cuts in the output of the KKMO reduction. This step, in turn, relies on a new, robust inverse Majority-Is-Stablest theorem.

papers.title: Parameterizing Cluster Editing by the Number of Deletions
papers.abstract: In Cluster Editing, we are given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$ and ask whether at most $k$ edge insertions and deletions turn $G$ into a disjoint union of cliques. Komusiewicz and Niedermeier asked in 2012 at MFCS whether Cluster Editing is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the number $\ell$ of edge deletions, a parameter based on the solution rather than on the structure of the input graph. We answer this question negatively: Cluster Editing with at most $k$ edits, at most $\ell$ of which are deletions, is W[1]-hard with respect to $\ell$, even when combined with the pathwidth and the feedback edge set number of the input graph. The hardness extends to editing towards $H$-free graphs for every graph $H$ that is a clique minus one edge on at least four vertices. On the positive side, we show that the problem becomes fixed-parameter tractable when $\ell$ is combined with the excess $\mu$ of $k$ over the lower bound given by a packing of modification-disjoint induced paths on three vertices, a lower bound that state-of-the-art solvers use. Each of the two parameters alone leads to intractability, but together they admit an $O(4^{\mu+\ell}\cdot(n+m+\mu))$-time algorithm and a problem kernel with $O((\ell+\mu)^2)$ vertices. Both results extend to packings of stars and the algorithm extends to $H$-free editing.

papers.title: Approximating Directed Telephone Multicast
papers.abstract: In the telephone model a message starts at a source vertex, and in every round each informed vertex may call one neighbour. Telephone multicast asks for a schedule that informs a given set of $k$ terminals in the fewest rounds. On directed graphs, the best known ratio for this problem was $\tilde O(\sqrt k)$, due to Elkin and Kortsarz and to Hathcock, Kortsarz and Ravi. For every integer $\ell\ge2$, we give a deterministic combinatorial algorithm with running time $n^{O(\ell)}$ that computes a schedule of length $O(\ell^3\log k)\cdot(\mathrm{OPT}+k^{1/\ell})$, where $n$ is the number of vertices and $\mathrm{OPT}$ the optimum. Since $\mathrm{OPT}\ge\log_2(k+1)$, this gives ratio $O(k^{\epsilon})$ in time $n^{O(1/\epsilon)}$ for every fixed $\epsilon>0$, and ratio $O(\log^4k)$ in quasi-polynomial time. The method rests on jump trees with additive vertex loads, a height reduction that bounds the load of every vertex, and a recursive greedy algorithm with an exponential potential. We also show that directed multicast is a special case of the degree-bounded directed Steiner tree problem on a time-expanded digraph. With known algorithms for that problem this gives randomized ratios $O(\log^2n)$ in time $n^{O(\log n)}$ and $O(n^\epsilon)$ in time $n^{O(1/\epsilon)}$, which, unlike ours, grow with $n$. On the hardness side, directed multicast stays $(1-\epsilon)\ln k$-hard even when $\mathrm{OPT}=O(\log k)$, the regime in which the previous algorithms were weakest.

papers.title: A 2/3-Approximation Algorithm for the Residual Maximum Matching Problem in General Graphs
papers.abstract: The residual maximum matching problem asks for a maximum matching whose deletion leaves a graph with the largest possible matching number. For unweighted graphs, previous work provides a $1/2$-approximation guarantee in general graphs and a $2/3$ guarantee in graphs with a perfect matching. We present a $2/3$-approximation algorithm running in $O(n^5)$ time, extending the latter guarantee to general graphs. The algorithm improves the residual matching number through single-edge exchanges involving free vertices. We prove that, for any maximum matching that admits no further improvement by such exchanges, the residual matching number is at least $2/3$ of the optimum, and we give an example showing that this bound is tight.

papers.title: An Exact Polynomial-Time Algorithm for the Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut Problem
papers.abstract: The Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut (MSPEC) problem seeks to disconnect two designated terminals with minimum total power by assigning powers to graph vertices and deleting every edge for which the sum of the powers at its endpoints reaches its edge weight. Previous work gave a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for this problem, while its exact computational complexity remained open. We prove that general MSPEC with nonnegative edge weights can be solved exactly in polynomial time. Specifically, we first use linear programming duality for each fixed cut to reformulate MSPEC as minimizing the maximum terminal-relaxed matching weight over all $s$-$t$ cuts. Then, we construct a terminal-copy extended graph that transforms the maximum-weight matching model with unconstrained terminal capacities for a fixed cut into an equivalent ordinary maximum-weight matching model. Next, we extend the submodularity of the unweighted maximum-matching cut function to nonnegative edge weights and prove that the restriction obtained by fixing the terminal copies on prescribed sides remains submodular. Consequently, MSPEC reduces to exact submodular function minimization. Once an optimal cut is obtained, a corresponding optimal power assignment can be recovered. This result resolves the open question concerning the exact computational complexity of general MSPEC.

papers.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Results for the Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set Problem
papers.abstract: We study the \emph{Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set} problem (MEG-Set), which asks for a minimum-cardinality set $M$ of vertices of an undirected graph $G$ of $n$ vertices such that every edge of $G$ belongs to all shortest paths between some pair of vertices in $M$. We present new approximation and hardness results for MEG-Set. On the positive side, we design a deterministic polynomial-time $O(n^{1/3}\log^{2/3}n)$-approximation algorithm, improving upon the previously best-known $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ approximation ratio. On the negative side, for every constant $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we prove that the problem admits no polynomial-time $\big(2^{\log^{1-\varepsilon} n}\big)$-approximation algorithm, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq \mathsf{DTIME}(n^{\operatorname{polylog} n})$. This substantially improves upon the previously known logarithmic inapproximability bound. We also prove that \megset is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard on planar $2$-degenerate graphs, whereas $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness was previously known for $1$-apex $2$-degenerate graphs. We conclude by observing a connection between monitoring edge-geodetic sets and subsetwise distance preservers, i.e., subgraphs that preserve distances between all pairs of vertices in $S\subseteq V(G)$. Specifically, we show that any upper bound on the size of the latter yields a lower bound on the size of the former.

papers.title: ARRIVAL in cube-root subexponential time
papers.abstract: In the ARRIVAL problem, a token travels through a switch digraph: at every vertex, it leaves along one of two out-arcs, and the two are used alternately. The question is which of two terminals the token reaches first. ARRIVAL lies in $\mathsf{NP} \cap \mathsf{coNP}$, but no polynomial-time algorithm is known.The fastest known algorithms turn some vertices into terminals and search for consistent guesses of the numbers of tokens that these vertices send out. The first, due to G\"artner et al. [ICALP 2021], searches all vertices at once with an algorithm for fixed points of monotone maps, and the second, due to Haslebacher [ICALP 2025], searches one vertex at a time by binary search. Both search for a fixed point of the same map, which returns how many tokens arrive at the guessed vertices. We guess the vertices in blocks of $k$, between these two extremes, which needs a search in $k$ dimensions with few evaluations of this map. To do so, we build on the connection between ARRIVAL and $\ell_1$-contractions established in the second of these works. We search with $\ell_1$-centerpoints of the remaining guesses, which are guaranteed to exist by Haslebacher et al. [FOCS 2025], and which we approximate deterministically. In order to prove our results, we show how to find the least fixed points of maps from $\{0, \ldots, N\}^k$ to itself that have unit increments. For ARRIVAL on $n$-vertex switch digraphs, this gives run time $2^{\mathcal{O}(n^{1/3} \cdot \log^{2/3} n)}$, improving the previous time bound of $n^{\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})}$. We work with the more general \garrival problem, with many tokens and several terminals, and solve it in the same time when there are at most $2^n$ tokens.

papers.title: Improved Approximation for Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Using Quota Trees
papers.abstract: In the Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (UCVRP), we are given a set $V$ of $n$ clients with normalized demands $d_v \in (0,1]$, a depot $r$, a unit vehicle capacity, and symmetric metric travel costs $c$ on $V \cup \{r\}$. We seek a collection of routes of minimum total cost that start and end at $r$, serve each client's entire demand on a single route, and respect the unit capacity constraint $\sum_{v \in V(R)} d_v \le 1$ on every route $R$, where $V(R)$ denotes the clients served by $R$. This models deliveries from a common depot in which each customer's order must be delivered in a single trip. UCVRP generalizes the metric traveling salesman problem (TSP) and is therefore NP-hard. Capacity constraints add a packing difficulty: when all clients are colocated away from the depot, minimizing the route cost is equivalent to minimizing the number of bins in bin packing. Consequently, UCVRP admits no polynomial-time approximation ratio below $3/2$ unless $\textbf{P=NP}$ (Grandoni, Mathieu, and Zhou, 2023). The classical $3.5$-approximation has been improved through several recent advances; in particular, Zhao and Xiao (2026) recently obtained a $(2+\ln 2+\varepsilon)$-approximation. In this paper, we give a deterministic $(5/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in $n^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ time for every rational $0<\varepsilon\le1/9$, applicable to general capacity and arbitrary positive demands. Our algorithm uses local search to select routes through one client with large demand and clients with small demands. It constructs candidate routes using endpoint quota trees after rounding demands and creating vertex copies. We combine these routes with those obtained by matching and set packing, keeping their client sets disjoint. The remaining clients are served by partitioning a tour constructed using weighted graphic matroid parity.

papers.title: Diverse Schedules for Makespan Minimization on Unrelated Machines
papers.abstract: We study makespan minimization on unrelated machines with the additional goal of constructing diverse schedules: Instead of outputting a single schedule, we seek a collection of schedules with provable makespan guarantees and substantially different job assignments. Committing to a single schedule in advance may be undesirable. Processing times may be uncertain, and constraints or domain knowledge may emerge later, so $k$ schedules of similar quality offer meaningful alternatives. We measure pairwise diversity by the weighted Hamming distance between job assignments and study the two standard objectives in the diverse-solutions literature: max-sum diversity, which maximizes the total pairwise distance between schedules, and max-min diversity, which maximizes the smallest pairwise distance. For the max-sum objective, we show that optimal diversity can be achieved in polynomial time without sacrificing the classic makespan approximation factor. For every feasible makespan target $T$, we can compute $k$ schedules of makespan at most $2T$ whose max-sum diversity is optimal among all $k$ schedules of makespan at most $T$. Therefore, we match the classic factor-$2$ makespan guarantee of Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos (Math. Prog., 1990) and preserve optimal diversity. For the max-min objective, we show that the diversity problem is inherently harder. Namely, we show that, even without makespan constraints, deciding whether three schedules of given pairwise diversity exist is NP-hard. We complete this with two complementary bicriteria approximation algorithms for every fixed $k$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. The first preserves almost all of the optimal max-min diversity with makespan at most $(3\lceil12/\varepsilon\rceil+1)T$. The second keeps the makespan arbitrarily close to the classic $2$ guarantee while achieving a $\frac{1}{2}(1-\varepsilon)$ fraction of the optimal max-min diversity.

papers.title: Dynamic Distances Without Matrix Inverse
papers.abstract: We study the fully dynamic exact distance problem in unweighted directed graphs, where the graph undergoes edge insertions and deletions, and the distance between two query vertices must be reported. Under the combinatorial Boolean matrix multiplication conjecture, any subquadratic-time algorithm for this problem must use algebraic techniques. All prior work uses the polynomial matrix inverse as its algebraic tool, but within subquadratic time, this technique can only maintain distances up to a small-polynomial hop bound. So larger distances must be reassembled from short-range pieces by a combinatorial layer. This hybrid algebraic-combinatorial construction has led to a substantial slowdown for dynamic distances compared to other dynamic graph problems relying on algebraic techniques. We give the first subquadratic-time dynamic distance algorithm built on dynamically maintaining a different algebraic object than the matrix inverse. By maintaining the Frobenius form $A=KCK^{-1}$ of a dynamic generic (i.e., cyclic) matrix $A$, we can query all the powers $A^\ell = K C^\ell K^{-1}$ efficiently. For adjacency matrix~$A$, the smallest $\ell$ with $(A^\ell)_{s,t}\neq 0$ is the $st$-distance in the associated graph. So, unlike dynamic matrix inverse, we get distance information directly without hop truncation, and we no longer need to perform any combinatorial reassembly. This purely algebraic approach to dynamic distances leads to the fastest dynamic distance algorithm with $O(n^{1.58})$ update time. The earlier use of the Frobenius form maintained the dense change of basis $K$ explicitly and required $\tilde O (n^2)$ time per update [KS23]. Our key observation is that this change of basis is highly structured, which lets us maintain it implicitly. This gives the first subquadratic dynamic algorithm for the Frobenius normal form and characteristic polynomial for generic matrices.

papers.title: Communication Complexity of Universal Features
papers.abstract: Motivated by the notion of features from machine learning, we study the complexity of representing data that allows for evaluation with a given family of functions. Concretely, we consider a deterministic encoder that observes $X\sim D$ and produces a finite encoding before a task $f\in\mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}$ is specified. For each task, a decoder must predict $f(X)$ with error at most $\varepsilon$ under $D$. We construct an encoder that outputs a representation with $O(d^{*}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ bits, where $d^{*}$ is the dual VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. Our encoder greedily selects $O((d^{*}/\varepsilon)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ functions from the class and uses their joint label pattern to produce the encoding. The key idea in our upper bound is a novel potential function argument, where we compare the entropy gained from each greedy selection with the number of patterns allowed by the dual VC dimension. We present lower bounds showing that the representation length achieved by our encoder is worst-case optimal for every $d^* \ge 1$ and $\varepsilon < 1/4$ up to a universal constant factor, and instance-wise optimal for every family $\mathcal{F}$ up to an $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ factor. We give two ways to learn the representation from unlabeled samples, with different guarantees on the representation size and sample complexity. Experimentally, we verify the greedy construction's accuracy-size tradeoff and explore its connection to neural sparse autoencoders.

papers.title: Improved rapid phase ordering for Ising dynamics on random regular graphs
papers.abstract: We study Glauber dynamics for the Ising model on random $d$-regular graphs with $n$ vertices at low temperature, in the regime $\beta \geq C/d$ where $C,d$ are sufficiently large constants. In this regime, the full mixing time is exponential in $n$, because of the bottleneck between the two dominant phases: configurations with a majority of plus spins and configurations with a majority of minus spins. We show that, for sufficiently large $d$, if the dynamics is initialized with an excess of at least $\epsilon_{C,d} n$ plus spins over minus spins, then it quasi-equilibrates in time $O(\log n)$ to the Gibbs measure conditioned on positive magnetization. In addition, the required bias $\epsilon_{C,d}$ can be chosen so that $\epsilon_{C,d}\to 0$ as $d,C\to\infty$. Previous bound of \cite{GSS25+} in the Ising and large-$d$ setting required $\beta \gtrsim (\log d)/d$. A key difficulty is that, even from the all-plus initialization, one must control the propagation of negative information in spacetime in a low-temperature model with strong local correlations. We address this by developing a new bootstrap approach to proving subcriticality of disagreement clusters under the grand coupling.

papers.title: Birthday Estimators Are Uniformly Optimal for Renyi Entropy
papers.abstract: Collisions are a basic probe of unknown distributions, used for testing and for counting substructures in graphs, and they underlie R\'enyi entropy, a fundamental measure of uncertainty with applications in cryptography, machine learning, physics, and biology. Motivated by this, we study the natural birthday estimator. We prove Bernstein-type concentration for it and show that it is minimax optimal, uniformly and jointly in alphabet size, order, accuracy, and confidence, with no sample splitting, clipping, or median aggregation. This, in particular, settles the sample complexity of integer-order R\'enyi entropy estimation up to absolute constants in all regimes, closing the gap between the best known upper and lower bounds. Our concentration bound rests on a sensitivity analysis of collision count, and the matching lower bound on a sharp analysis of detecting a hidden spike in a plateau distribution.

papers.title: Assortment optimization given basket shopping behavior using the Ising model
papers.abstract: In markets where customers tend to purchase baskets of products rather than single products, assortment optimization is a major challenge for retailers. Removing a product from a retailer's assortment can result in a severe drop in aggregate demand if this product is a complement to other products. Therefore, accounting for the complementarity effect is essential when making assortment decisions. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework designed to address this problem. We model customers' choices using the binary Ising model, which is a special case of a Markov random field. This model captures pairwise demand dependencies as well as the individual attractiveness of each product, with binary variables indicating whether products are included in the purchased basket. For estimation, we utilize existing methods developed for the spin formulation of the Ising model and then apply a parameter transformation to express the fitted model in the binary form used for assortment optimization. We show that the assortment optimization problem under the Ising model is NP-hard. We also provide multiple theoretical insights into the structure of the optimal assortments based on the graphical representation of the Ising model, and propose several heuristic algorithms that can be used to obtain high-quality solutions to the assortment optimization problem. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the developed simulated annealing procedure leads to an expected profit gain of 15% compared to offering an unoptimized assortment (where all products are included) and around 5% compared to using a revenue-ordered heuristic algorithm.

papers.title: Verified Purely Functional Catenable Real-Time Deques
papers.abstract: We present OCaml and Rocq implementations of Kaplan and Tarjan's purely functional, real-time catenable deques. The correctness of our Rocq code is machine-checked.

papers.title: Moment Ambiguity and the Limits of Robust Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: We study fundamental information-theoretic limits of robust stochastic optimization when the distribution is known only through its exact moment sequence. We develop a unified framework that produces families of distinct distributions sharing all moments yet inducing radically different optimal decisions, thereby establishing strong impossibility results for a range of decision problems under moment ambiguity. Our binary and $N$-way moment-matching constructions separate quantiles, threshold regions, and online selection opportunities while preserving every moment. For the newsvendor problem, moment equivalence causes quantile ambiguity, inducing any fixed or randomized order quantity to fail arbitrarily badly. For revenue maximization, no deterministic or randomized posted pricing scheme can secure a nontrivial approximation relative to the full-information benchmark. For the secretary problem with cardinal observations, the optimal robust success probability under exact moment disclosure is the classical finite-horizon value $s_m$, even for i.i.d. observations. This value converges to $1/e$, compared with the full-information limit of approximately $0.5801$ due to Gilbert and Mosteller (J. Am. Stat. Assoc., 1966). We also recover and expand upon the recent impossibility result of Correa et al. (STOC, 2026) for prophet inequalities with moment knowledge. For every fixed $r\ge1$, exact moment knowledge can yield at best a $\Theta(1/\log m)$ competitive ratio, even when competing against relaxed benchmarks based on expected $r$-th order statistics or when the algorithm is allowed to select $r$ items.

papers.title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning
papers.abstract: We study multi-robot motion planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots. The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain $\mathcal{W}$ with $n$ vertices and $k$ robots $R_1,\dots,R_k$ translating in $\mathcal{W}$ each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity. Given a source configuration $\mathbf{s}$ and a target configuration $\mathbf{t}$ of the robots in $\mathcal{W}$, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ that is shortest with respect to some cost function. We present the first fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTAS) for motion planning with any fixed number $k$ of robots, under the min-sum objective, the min-max objective, and the min-makespan objective. Here, the min-sum variant aims to minimize the total traveling distance of all robots, the min-max variant aims to minimize the maximum traveling distance of a single robot, and the min-makespan variant aims to minimize the total time cost under the assumption that all robots move with a maximum speed $1$. The algorithm directly generalizes to the problem in any fixed dimension $d$, with a polytope environment and polytope robots. Our result settles an open question of Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, Steiger [SODA'24] and Agarwal, Holmgren, Steiger [SODA'26], who gave an FPTAS for $k=2$ unit-square robots and a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for a fixed number $k$ of unit-square or unit-disk robots, respectively. Compared to the previous results, our algorithm is substantially simpler.

papers.title: Shaving Logs via Large Sieve Inequality: Faster Algorithms for Sparse Convolution and More
papers.abstract: In sparse convolution-type problems, a common technique is to hash the input integers modulo a random prime $p\in [Q/2,Q]$ for some parameter $Q$, which reduces the range of the input integers while preserving their additive structure. However, this hash family suffers from two drawbacks, which led to bottlenecks in many state-of-the-art algorithms: (1) The collision probability of two elements from $[N]$ is $O(\frac{\log N}{Q})$ rather than $O(\frac{1}{Q})$; (2) It is difficult to derandomize the choice of $p$; known derandomization techniques lead to super-logarithmic overhead [Chan, Lewenstein STOC'15]. In this paper, we partially overcome these drawbacks in certain scenarios, via novel applications of the large sieve inequality from analytic number theory. Consequently, we obtain the following improved algorithms for various problems (in the standard word RAM model): Sparse Nonnegative Convolution: We obtain an $O(t\log t)$-time Las Vegas algorithm that computes the convolution $A\star B$ of two nonnegative integer vectors $A,B$, where $t$ is the output sparsity $\|A\star B\|_0$. Moreover, our algorithm terminates in $O(t\log t)$ time with $1-1/\mathrm{poly}(t)$ probability. Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances: Given a length-$m$ pattern $P$ and a length-$n$ text $T$, we obtain a deterministic $O(n\sqrt{m\log \log m})$-time algorithm that exactly computes the Hamming distance between $P$ and every length-$m$ substring of $T$. Sparse General Convolution: We also give a Monte Carlo $O(t\log t)$ time algorithm for sparse convolution with possibly negative input in the restricted case where the length $N$ of the input vectors satisfies $N\le t^{1.99}$.

papers.title: ${\varepsilon}$-Cost Sharding: Scaling Hypergraph-Based Data Structures to Trillions of Keys
papers.abstract: We describe a simple and yet very scalable implementation of static functions (VFunc) and of static filters (VFilter) based on hypergraphs. We introduce the idea of $\varepsilon$-cost sharding, which allows us to build structures that can manage trillions of keys, at the same time increasing memory locality in hypergraph-based constructions. Contrarily to the commonly used HEM sharding method, $\varepsilon$-cost sharding does not require to store of additional information, and does not introduce dependencies in the computation chain; its only cost is that of few arithmetical instructions, and of a relative increase $\varepsilon$ in space usage. We apply $\varepsilon$-cost sharding to the classical MWHC construction, but we obtain the best result by combining Dietzfelbinger and Walzer's fuse graphs for large shards with lazy Gaussian elimination for small shards. We obtain large structures with an overhead of 10.5% with respect to the information-theoretical lower bound and with a query time that is a few nanoseconds away from the query time of the non-sharded version, which is the fastest currently available within the same space bounds. Besides comparing our structures with a non-sharded version, we contrast its tradeoffs with bumped ribbon constructions, a space-saving alternative to hypergraph-based static functions and filters, which provide optimum space consumption but slow construction and query time (though construction can be parallelized very efficiently). We build offline a trillion-key filter using commodity hardware in just 60 ns/key. Finally, we show that $\varepsilon$-cost sharding and fuse graphs carry over with no effort to data structures that reduce to static functions, such as monotone minimal perfect hash functions and compressed static functions.

papers.title: Algorithms for Computing Longest Unbordered Factors on Run-Length Encoded Strings
papers.abstract: A border of a string is a non-empty proper prefix of the string that is also a suffix. A string is called unbordered if it has no border. The longest unbordered factor is a fundamental notion in stringology, closely related to string periodicity. This paper addresses the longest unbordered factor problem: given a string of length $n$, the goal is to compute its longest factor that is unbordered. While recent work has achieved subquadratic and near-linear time algorithms for this problem, the best known worst-case time complexity remains $O(n \log n)$ [Kociumaka et al., ISAAC 2018]. In this paper, we investigate the problem in the context of compressed string processing, focusing specifically on run-length encoded (RLE) strings. We first present a simple yet crucial structural observation relating unbordered factors and RLE-compressed strings. Building on this, we propose an algorithm that solves the problem in $O(m^{1.5} \log^2 m)$ time and $O(m \log^2 m)$ space, where $m$ is the size of the RLE-compressed input string. Furthermore, we propose another algorithm for the problem that runs in average $O(m \log^2 m)$ time and $O(m\log m)$ space: The average-case bound holds under an exponent-bounded random-input model, in which the input is chosen uniformly from the strings of RLE size $m$ whose run exponents are at most a given bound $E\geq 2$. Our approaches extend key ideas from [Gawrychowski et al., SPIRE 2015] to the RLE setting through new combinatorial insights. When the RLE size $m$ is sufficiently small compared to $n$, our algorithms achieve linear-time behavior in $n$, potentially leading to improved performance over existing methods in such cases.

papers.title: Improved Online Load Balancing in the Two-Norm
papers.abstract: We study the online load balancing problem on unrelated machines, with the objective of minimizing the square of the $\ell_2$ norm of the loads on the machines. The greedy algorithm of Awerbuch et al. (STOC'95) is optimal for deterministic algorithms and achieves a competitive ratio of $3 + 2 \sqrt{2} \approx 5.828$, and an improved $5$-competitive randomized algorithm based on independent rounding has been shown by Caragiannis (SODA'08). In this work, we present the first algorithm breaking the barrier of $5$ on the competitive ratio, achieving a bound of $5-c$ for some $c \geq 0.0157$. To obtain this result, we use a new primal-dual framework to analyze this problem based on a natural semidefinite programming relaxation, together with an online implementation of a correlated randomized rounding procedure of Im and Shadloo (SODA'20). This novel primal-dual framework also yields new, simple and unified proofs of the competitive ratio of the $(3 + 2 \sqrt{2})$-competitive greedy algorithm, the $5$-competitive randomized independent rounding algorithm, and that of a new $4$-competitive optimal fractional algorithm. We also provide lower bounds showing that the previous best randomized algorithm is optimal among independent rounding algorithms, that our new fractional algorithm is optimal, and that a simple greedy algorithm is optimal for the closely related online scheduling problem $R || \sum w_j C_j$.

papers.title: Simpler Logarithmic Approximation Algorithms for the Optimal Decision Tree and Adaptive Set Cover
papers.abstract: We study the problem of constructing a decision tree that identifies an unknown hypothesis from a given ground set, under both average- and worst-case cost. The Optimal Decision Tree (ODT) problem has been extensively studied in the literature, and $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$-approximation guarantees are known for each criterion, including a simultaneous guarantee for both (here $n$ is the number of hypotheses) [ICML]. Although most of the existing algorithm use simple greedy strategies, their analyses rely on intricate arguments. Since ODT is a fundamental problem with wide-ranging applications, we are interested in developing algorithms that are both effective and easy to understand. We present a new greedy algorithm with a simplified analysis that simultaneously achieves approximation factors below $3.65\log_2 n$ for worst-case cost and $7.3\log_2 n$ for average-case cost. Our algorithm for the Optimal Decision Tree behaves greedily with respect to the hereby introduced Separating Subfamily problem which asks for the cheapest subfamily of tests which partitions the hypotheses into pieces of small enough size. We show that the Separating Subfamily can itself be reduced to an instance of the well-known Maximum Coverage problem. At the core of our approach lies exploiting properties of cutting a clique into small pieces, where edges represent pairs of hypotheses to be separated. In the spirit of simplicity, we also provide a new and straightforward application of ODT: an $\mathcal{O}(\log (k\cdot n))$-approximation for the Adaptive Set Cover problem, where $k$ is the number of possible realizations.

papers.title: Connected (Dense) Partition for Tree-Like Graphs
papers.abstract: We focus on two variants of graph partitioning problems, connected partition and dense partition. Formally, given a graph $G=(V,E)$ and a partition of its vertices $\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots, P_k\}$ we say that $\mathcal P$ is a connected partition of $G$ if each $P_i$ induces a connected graph in $G$. Many classical variants of this problem impose additional restrictions both on the number of parts as well as on the size of each part. Moreover, given a partition $\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots, P_k\}$ we define its density by $d(\mathcal P):=\sum_{i=1}^k |E(P_i)|/|V(P_i)|$. The problem Maximum Dense Graph Partition asks to construct a partition of maximum density. We study this problem both with and without fixed number of sets $k$. We prove the following results: 1. A polynomial time algorithm for \textsc{Maximum Dense Graph Partition} of thick forests, a subclass of chordal graphs, generalizing the previously known polynomial time algorithm on block graphs. 2. A generic dynamic programming algorithm to construct (if possible) a connected partition into $k$ sets of prescribed sizes on graphs with bounded treewidth. This yields algorithms for both variants of Dense Graph Partition and an efficient construction for the Gy\H{o}ri-Lov\'{a}sz theorem. 3. The $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness of Maximum Dense Graph Partition restricted to split graphs, showing that thick trees are a boundary for the polynomial computability of this problem.
